sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Njord** ​(*njord*) — ‌The Sea, ‌Wealth, the ​Vanir Hostage ​· ​Variant — ​belongs to ​the Norse ‌tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Sea, ‌Wind, ​Wealth". The ‌name means ​"Variant: plain ​anglicization (no ​o-slash)"[^1].

​**Njǫrðr** is ​the Norse ‌sea-god of ​the ‌safe shore: ​the Vanir ‌hostage who ​chose the ‌sea-cliffs ​over the ‌mountains, father ​of Freyr ​and ‌Freyja, giver ‌of wealth ‌and fair ​winds to ​sailors ‌and merchants. ​He is ​the gods’ ‌peacemaker — ​the ​hostage-exchange that ‌ended the ​Æsir–Vanir war ‌made ​him the ​divine guarantee ​that treaties ​hold, and ‌the ‌sea’s temper ​mirrors his: ‌calm, rich, ​and implacable ​when ‌crossed.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ‌canonical scholarly ‌spelling ​**Njord** and ‌serves its ​temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/njord/). ​The ‌displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *njord* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌written attestation ‌survives ​for ​this name; ​**Njord** ​is ​a scholarly ‌transliteration ​of ​the reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. ‌Etymologically the ​name ‌means ​"Variant: plain ​anglicization ​(no ​o-slash)"[^1].

The ​canonical ‌spelling ​**Njord** matches ‌the ​conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ​ASCII form ‌*njord* ​contains ​the same ‌letters, ‌so ‌no lost ​diacritics ​or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ‌reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization ​and provenance, ‌and ‌keep ​the original ‌evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ‌form ‌is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ‌a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed ​form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**n** ‌→ ​**N** — ​Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**j** → ​**j** ‌— ​Same
- **o** ‌→ ​**o** ‌— Same
- ‌**r** ​→ ​**r** — ​Same
- ​**d** ‌→ **d** ‌— ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name ​is **/ˈnjɔːrd/** ​— ​Old Norse ​(normalised).[^1]

Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

- **Nj-** ​— ​The nj ‌is a ​palatalised ‌n — ​“ny” ‌as in ​“canyon”; the ​vowel ​å as ​in ​“or”.
- **-ǫrð** ‌— The ​final ‌ð is ​the ‌soft “th” ​of “this” ‌— ​“NYORTH”. The ‌anglicised ​“Njord” keeps ​only the ‌n.
- ‌**** — ‌The ​Old Norse ​form carries ‌the ​palatal and ​the ‌soft ð; ​the plain ​anglicisation ‌is a ​separate ‌lexicon entry.

​For the ​modern ​speaker, the ​closest ‌approximation is: ‌“NYORTH” — ​palatal ‌n, soft ​th ​ending

Kindred ‌and historical ‌forms ‌of the ‌name:

- ​**Anglicised** — ‌Njord — ​the ​plain form, ​kept ‌as a ​separate lexicon ​entry
- ​**Lineage** — ‌father ​of Freyr ​and Freyja; ​the ‌Vanir hostage ​among ‌the Æsir

​The name ‌may ​be related ‌to ‌the Germanic ​Nerthus of ​Tacitus’ ​Germania — ​the ‌earth-goddess of ‌the first-century ​North.

sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Njǫrðr** ​is the ‌Norse sea-god ‌of the ​safe shore: ​the ​Vanir hostage ​who chose ​the sea-cliffs ‌over ​the mountains, ​father of ‌Freyr and ​Freyja, giver ‌of ​wealth and ‌fair winds ​to sailors ​and merchants. ​He ​is the ​gods’ peacemaker ‌— the ​hostage-exchange ‌that ended ​the Æsir–Vanir ‌war made ​him the ‌divine ​guarantee that ‌treaties hold, ​and the ​sea’s ‌temper mirrors ‌his: calm, ‌rich, and ​implacable when ​crossed.[^1]

### ‌Lord of ​the Coast

​He rules ‌the sea’s ​edge ​and the ‌fair wind ​— sailors ‌and ​merchants call ​on him ​for safe ​passage and ‌good ‌trade.

### The ​Hostage of ‌Peace

Given ​to the ​Æsir ‌to seal ‌the peace ‌with the ‌Vanir; ​the gods’ ‌own guarantee ​that oaths ​bind.

### Father ​of ‌the Twins

​Freyr and ​Freyja are ​his ‌children by ​his sister ​— the ​Vanir marriage-custom ‌the ​Æsir could ‌not accept.

### ​Giver of ‌Wealth

Sea-wealth ​flows ‌from him ‌— the ​Norse word ​for ​wealth and ​the sea’s ‌gift are ‌his domain ​together.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Njord ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ​of recurring ‌attributes, ​each ​a ‌compressed statement ​about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- **Lord ‌of ​the ​Coast** ​— He ​rules ​the ‌sea’s edge ​and ‌the ​fair wind ‌— ​sailors ‌and ​merchants call ‌on ​him ​for safe ‌passage ‌and ‌good ​trade.
- **The ​Hostage ‌of ​Peace** — ​Given ‌to ​the Æsir ​to ‌seal ​the ‌peace with ​the ​Vanir; ​the gods’ ​own ‌guarantee ‌that oaths ​bind.
- ‌**Father ​of ​the Twins** ‌— ‌Freyr ‌and Freyja ‌are ​his ‌children ​by his ​sister ​— ‌the Vanir ​marriage-custom ​the ​Æsir could ‌not ​accept.
- ​**Giver ​of Wealth** ‌— ​Sea-wealth ‌flows from ​him ‌— ​the ‌Norse word ‌for ​wealth ​and the ​sea’s ​gift ‌are his ‌domain ​together.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Njǫrðr’s mythology ​is the peace-myth: the ‌hostage-exchange that ended the ‌gods’ first war, and ​the marriage that ​failed across the divine ​factions. His two stories ​— the Æsir–Vanir peace ​and the nine ‌nights with Skaði — ​are the Norse pantheon’s ​domestic politics, and both ‌end in the ​same lesson: some bonds ‌hold, and some were ​never possible.[^1]

### The Æsir–Vanir ‌Peace (Gylfaginning)

The ​first war in the ​world — Æsir against ​Vanir — ended not ​in victory but ​in exchange: Njǫrðr and ‌his children went to ​the Æsir, and the ‌Vanir received Hœnir ​and Mímir in return. ‌Snorri notes the exchange’s ​unevenness (the Vanir beheaded ‌Mímir in disgust) ​and its durability: Njǫrðr ‌became the Æsir’s own ​sea-lord, the living treaty ​between the divine ‌races.[^2]

### The Nine Nights ‌with Skaði (Skáldskaparmál)

Skaði, ‌the ski-goddess, chose her ​husband by his ​feet among the veiled ‌gods — she reached ​for Baldr and got ​Njǫrðr. Their marriage ‌split on geography: he ​could not sleep in ​her mountain halls, where ‌the wolves’ howling ​kept him from rest; ‌she could not sleep ​by the sea, where ​the gulls’ crying ​drove her mad. Nine ​nights in each home, ‌then the parting — ‌the gods’ most ​honest divorce.

### The Flyting’s ‌Accusations (Lokasenna)

Loki’s taunting ​catalogue in the gods’ ​hall accuses Njǫrðr ‌of fathering his children ‌on his own sister ‌— the Vanir custom ‌the Æsir condemned ​— and of letting ‌the hostage’s price be ​paid in shame. Njǫrðr’s ​answer is dignity ​itself: ‘small harm in ‌a lover, when sisters ​and husbands are beyond ​the gods’ borders’ ​— the hostage’s quiet ‌defense of his people’s ​ways.

### The Earth-Before-the-Sea (Tacitus’ ​Nerthus)

Tacitus’ Germania ​describes the North’s first-century ‌goddess Nerthus — an ​earth-deity drawn in a ‌covered wagon, feasted, ​and drowned in her ‌lake in secret rites. ​Linguists and historians of ‌religion long ago ‌set Njǫrðr and Nerthus ​side by side: the ​same divine name, perhaps, ​before the sea ​claimed the land’s share ‌— the gender and ‌the element exchanged across ​the centuries.
